L2t: The Speech or Debate Clause in Article I, Section 6 protects members of Congress for legislative acts, and courts have applied it to bar civil suits as well as criminal prosecutions.
L3t: Because a floor speech is a core legislative act, the Speech or Debate Clause makes the senator absolutely immune from civil liability for it, whether or not the statement was false or negligent.
L4t: The court should dismiss because the Speech or Debate Clause of Article I, Section 6 absolutely immunizes the senator from defamation liability for statements made on the Senate floor.
L2f: Sovereign immunity in the United States rests on the Eleventh Amendment, which since ratification has barred all suits against any government official, federal or state, for damages.
L3f: The suit is in substance a claim against the United States, because a senator speaking on the floor acts only as an agent of the federal government, so the government's immunity from suit governs the claim.
L4f: The court should dismiss because the federal government is constitutionally immune from suit without its consent, and it has not consented to defamation suits of this kind.
cand_true: Speech or Debate Clause immunity for the senator's floor statements
cand_wrong1: Federal sovereign immunity with no governmental consent to suit
cand_wrong2: The purchasing officer is a public official who must plead actual malice under New York Times v. Sullivan
